screens.title: Understanding Snowflake Editions & Pricing Model
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how Snowflake’s editions and its consumption-based pricing shape what you can do and the cost you pay. Snowflake offers distinct editions — Standard, Enterprise, Business Critical, and Virtual Private Snowflake — each providing progressively stronger features for concurrency, recovery, and compliance. Understanding those differences helps you pick the right trade-off between capability and price. Equally important is Snowflake’s billing model: storage charges for average compressed data retained, compute billed as credits while virtual warehouses run, and a Cloud Services layer that normally is included but can be charged for extreme metadata activity. Throughout this chapter you’ll see concrete examples: credit rates by warehouse size, the effect of Time Travel and Fail-safe on storage, and common mistakes that lead to unexpected bills. You’ll also learn practical controls — auto-suspend, right-sizing, and zero-copy cloning — that reduce cost without sacrificing productivity. By the end, you’ll be able to map a business requirement to an edition choice and a cost-control plan. Consider which feature matters most to your organization: concurrency, compliance, or isolation?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Understanding Snowflake Editions
Understanding Snowflake Editions & Pricing Model
How edition choice and consumption-based billing affect features, compliance, and costs.
In this lesson
Compare editions, read cost drivers for storage and compute, and learn optimization controls like auto-suspend and zero-copy cloning.
Why it matters
Choosing the wrong edition or leaving warehouses running are common causes of unexpected bills and operational gaps in compliance and availability.
Quick orientation

Edition = features & compliance. Storage = TB/month. Compute = credits while warehouses run. Cloud Services usually included.

Edition & Cost Snapshot
Standard → Enterprise → Business Critical → VPS
Standard
Core features, basic security, suitable for small teams.
Enterprise
Multi-cluster, longer Time Travel, materialized views.
Business Critical
Advanced compliance, Tri-Secret Secure, failover.
Explore key topics below to get to practical controls and monitoring steps you can apply today.
Storage Costs
Charged per TB/month, includes Time Travel and Fail-safe snapshots.
Compute Credits
Warehouses consume credits while running; size determines rate.
Optimization
Auto-suspend, right-size, and zero-copy cloning cut costs significantly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the appropriate Snowflake edition for a given requirement, explain how storage and compute contribute to your bill, and use practical controls to limit cost. First, you will differentiate Standard, Enterprise, Business Critical, and VPS editions by features and compliance needs. For example, you'll recognize when multi-cluster warehouses or Tri-Secret Secure are required. Second, you will identify the cost drivers: average compressed storage billed per month, compute billed as credits while warehouses run, and the Cloud Services layer that usually is included but may be charged for extreme metadata use. Third, you will explain optimization strategies such as right-sizing warehouses, enabling auto-suspend, and using zero-copy cloning to avoid duplicate storage costs. Finally, you will monitor resource usage in Snowsight and interpret credit and storage charts to make decisions. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competency by checking usage charts and applying a suspension on a test warehouse. These skills help teams avoid common billing surprises while maintaining performance and compliance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Learning Objectives — Implementation
Verify Usage in Snowsight
Open Admin → Usage and inspect the Credit Usage and Storage Usage charts.
Check the time range, identify spikes, and note which warehouses consumed credits. This confirms how compute patterns map to spend.
Test Auto-Suspend
Suspend a test warehouse and observe credit usage stopping shortly after suspension.
This demonstrates compute billing is tied to active warehouse time and validates savings from suspension.
Inspect Storage Retention
Compare Average Storage and Fail-safe usage and reason about Time Travel retention impact.
Longer Time Travel increases stored historical data and monthly storage charges; Fail-safe is non-configurable and billed as well.
Map Requirements to Edition
Practice mapping concurrency, recovery duration, and compliance needs to editions.
This helps avoid picking an underpowered edition or overspending on unnecessary isolation.

screens.title: What are Snowflake Editions?
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake editions are packaged service tiers that expose different features and levels of isolation to match organizational needs. At its base, the Standard edition supplies the fully managed warehouse with separate storage and compute, secure sharing, and encryption. Enterprise adds operational capabilities such as multi-cluster warehouses to handle concurrency, longer Time Travel retention up to 90 days, and materialized views to improve query performance. Business Critical layers on compliance and advanced encryption controls like Tri-Secret Secure and database failover for disaster recovery. Virtual Private Snowflake provides a fully isolated Snowflake deployment for extreme security and regulatory requirements. A practical example: a small analytics team without strict regulatory needs commonly starts on Standard to avoid paying for advanced compliance features they won't use. A bank that needs HIPAA, PCI DSS, or FedRAMP will consider Business Critical or VPS to meet audits and control encryption keys. A common misconception is thinking edition selection only affects security; in reality it also changes operational capabilities such as concurrency, recovery time windows, and metadata isolation. Key takeaway: match edition choice to real requirements — concurrency and recovery point needs, and compliance obligations — rather than choosing the highest edition by default. Which dimension—concurrency, compliance, or full isolation—matters most for your workload?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Editions group features and compliance levels so you can align costs to business requirements.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What are Snowflake Editions?
Edition definitions
  • Standard: Core warehouse features, basic security.
  • Enterprise: Multi-cluster, extended Time Travel, materialized views.
  • Business Critical: Advanced compliance, Tri-Secret Secure, failover.
  • VPS: Dedicated Snowflake instance for maximum isolation.
Key Takeaway

Choose the edition that aligns with required compliance and operational features, not by default to the highest tier.

Concrete scenario
A retailer with thousands of daily concurrent BI queries may need Enterprise for multi-cluster warehouses. A healthcare provider processing PHI may require Business Critical for compliance and Tri-Secret Secure.
Common mistake
Selecting a higher edition for perceived safety without mapping features to needs increases cost unnecessarily.
Check your understanding
List the top requirement for your project: concurrency, compliance, or isolation. Which edition answers that primary need?

screens.title: Standard vs Enterprise — When to upgrade
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing Standard and Enterprise editions helps you decide when to upgrade as usage grows. Standard provides the managed data warehouse, encryption in transit and at rest, separate storage and compute, and secure data sharing — good for smaller teams and general analytics work. Enterprise adds features for scale and recovery: multi-cluster warehouses to handle higher concurrency without queuing, longer Time Travel retention up to 90 days for extended recovery windows, and materialized views to speed frequent queries. Consider a concrete example: if an analytics team experiences frequent query queueing during business hours, Enterprise’s multi-cluster capability can spin additional compute to serve concurrent users. A misconception is assuming Enterprise only improves performance; it also extends recovery options and supports different operational patterns like larger, more concurrent workloads. Another common pitfall is over-provisioning: upgrading before you measure concurrency or Time Travel needs can lead to unnecessary spend. Key takeaway: measure concurrency and recovery requirements first, and then apply Enterprise capabilities where real demand exists. Which workload metric will you check to justify an upgrade? Standard vs Enterprise — When to upgrade means upgrade to enterprise when concurrency and extended recovery or materialized views are required.. In practical terms, concurrency, time travel, and materialized views explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Standard vs Enterprise
Standard Edition
Core features for most analytics, separate storage and compute, basic retention and security.
  • Good for small-to-medium workloads
  • Default Time Travel shorter (configurable)
  • Lower baseline cost compared to higher editions
Enterprise Edition
Adds multi-cluster warehouses, up to 90 days Time Travel, and materialized views for performance.
  • Handles high concurrency better
  • Longer recovery windows
  • Improves repeat-query performance with materialized views
Concrete example

If dashboards queue during peak hours, measure concurrency. If queues exceed thresholds, multi-cluster warehouses in Enterprise can scale out automatically to reduce wait time.

screens.title: Business Critical & Tri-Secret Secure
screens.narratorSegment: Business Critical edition focuses on advanced security and compliance for regulated industries. It includes support for standards like HIPAA, PCI DSS, and FedRAMP and provides stronger controls including Tri-Secret Secure and client-side encryption options. Tri-Secret Secure gives you additional control over encryption key management so an organization can meet strict key-handling requirements. Business Critical also includes database failover and failback to improve business continuity. A concrete use case is a healthcare provider that must meet HIPAA rules and control encryption keys; Business Critical offers the features and contractual support to align operations to those obligations. A common misconception is that encryption at rest and in transit alone satisfy all audits; many audits require documented key control and failover capabilities, which Business Critical adds. Key takeaway: choose Business Critical when your compliance requirements specify key management, certified standards, or contractual obligations that go beyond standard protections. Reflect on which audit controls your organization actually needs before selecting this edition. Business Critical & Tri-Secret Secure means business critical elevates security and key control to meet regulated-industry audit and continuity requirements.. In practical terms, advanced security, compliance, and key management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

What Business Critical adds
  • Compliance certifications (HIPAA, PCI DSS, FedRAMP)
  • Tri-Secret Secure for enhanced key management
  • Database failover and failback for continuity
This edition is appropriate when audits and contractual obligations require documented encryption and failover controls beyond basic protections.
Concrete example
A healthcare organization needs documented key separation and failover testing to meet HIPAA. Business Critical supports these needs.
Key Takeaway

Use Business Critical when audits require advanced key control and failover capabilities.

screens.title: Virtual Private Snowflake (VPS)
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual Private Snowflake, or VPS, provides the highest degree of isolation by running your Snowflake account on a dedicated instance separated from other customers. This includes dedicated metadata storage and compute resources which helps organizations with stringent regulatory or contractual isolation requirements. VPS is typically reserved for very large enterprises or government agencies that cannot accept any multi-tenant risk. A concrete scenario is a government agency that mandates physical separation of metadata and compute from public multi-tenant clouds; VPS offers that segregated environment. Important to understand is the trade-off: VPS delivers maximal control and isolation but increases cost and operational boundaries compared to multi-tenant editions. A common misconception is assuming VPS is merely a performance boost — it is primarily an isolation and security construct. Key takeaway: choose VPS only when policy or law requires dedicated service boundaries, and validate whether your compliance needs cannot be met by Business Critical before selecting VPS. Virtual Private Snowflake (VPS) means vps gives dedicated resources and metadata separation for organizations that require maximum isolation.. In practical terms, dedicated snowflake instance for maximum isolation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Virtual Private Snowflake
What VPS provides
  • Dedicated Snowflake service instance
  • Isolated metadata and compute resources
  • Designed for agencies and very large enterprises with strict isolation needs
VPS is a specialized option and not necessary for most organizations. Evaluate contractual and legal separation requirements first.
Example
A government body that requires a fully segregated metadata service and dedicated compute would consider VPS.
Key Takeaway

VPS is for extreme isolation; choose it only when policy or law demands dedicated infrastructure.

screens.title: Storage Costs — How you are billed
screens.narratorSegment: Storage cost in Snowflake is based on the average amount of compressed data you store per month. That monthly average includes live table data, historical data retained for Time Travel, and data stored for Fail-safe. For example, storing 10 terabytes means you are billed for 10 TB of storage regardless of how often that data is queried. Time Travel increases stored data because historical versions are maintained; so longer retention windows raise monthly storage usage. Fail-safe is a non-configurable seven-day period used for disaster recovery and its storage is billed as well. A common mistake is underestimating storage impact from extended Time Travel settings or clones that create many changed blocks — while zero-copy cloning avoids duplicating full datasets, changes to the clone do consume additional storage. Practical steps to control storage costs include keeping Time Travel retention reasonable for your recovery needs and leveraging zero-copy cloning for development and testing. Key takeaway: storage charges reflect what you keep, not what you query — review retention settings to control recurring costs. How long do you actually need historical versions for your workflows?

keyIdea.title: Storage billing
keyIdea.text: You pay for average compressed data stored each month, including Time Travel and Fail-safe.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Storage Costs
Billing components
  • Average compressed storage billed per month (per TB).
  • Time Travel retains historical data and increases storage usage.
  • Fail-safe is a mandatory 7-day retention for disaster recovery and is billed.
Example
Storing 10 TB results in charges for 10 TB that month, and increasing Time Travel will raise that average.
Key Takeaway

Control retention windows and use zero-copy clones to reduce duplicate storage while keeping recovery capabilities.

screens.title: Compute Costs & Virtual Warehouses
screens.narratorSegment: Compute costs are charged based on virtual warehouse usage, measured in credits consumed while warehouses are running. Warehouse sizes map to credits per hour: an X-Small consumes 1 credit per hour, Small 2, Medium 4, and so on, doubling with each size step. Crucially, you are billed only when the warehouse is active. That’s why controls like AUTO_SUSPEND and AUTO_RESUME are central to cost control. Configure AUTO_SUSPEND to a low idle timeout such as five to ten minutes so warehouses stop when not needed. A common mistake is leaving a warehouse running overnight or choosing a large warehouse to avoid occasional latency, both of which increase credits consumed unnecessarily. For example, if a team repeatedly runs short ETL jobs, an X-Small or Small with quick auto-suspend will cost far less than a larger size that runs continuously. Key takeaway: monitor active warehouse uptime and right-size for the workload. Ask yourself: can this workload run on a smaller size or be scheduled to start only when needed? Compute Costs & Virtual Warehouses means credits are consumed only when warehouses run; size and runtime determine cost, so auto-suspend and right-sizing are essential.. In practical terms, how credits are consumed and why auto-suspend matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Compute Costs & Warehouses
Credit consumption by size
  • X-Small = 1 credit/hour
  • Small = 2 credits/hour
  • Medium = 4 credits/hour
  • Each size doubles the credits of the previous one
Controls to reduce compute spend
  • Enable AUTO_SUSPEND (5–10 minutes recommended)
  • Use AUTO_RESUME to start on demand
  • Right-size warehouses to match workload
Concrete example

Short ETL jobs are cheaper on an X-Small with a 5-minute auto-suspend than on a large warehouse that is left running between jobs.

screens.title: Cloud Services Costs
screens.narratorSegment: The Cloud Services layer contains Snowflake’s control plane: authentication, metadata management, query parsing and optimization, and other coordination functions. For most customers, Cloud Services cost is included within compute usage. However, Snowflake may bill Cloud Services separately if usage of this layer is disproportionate to compute — for instance, when millions of tiny queries generate a lot of metadata activity that doesn't consume much warehouse compute. This separate billing is rare for typical workloads, but it illustrates that metadata-heavy patterns can influence cost beyond storage and compute. A concrete example is an environment with many small metadata-only operations or frequent session churn; such patterns may push Cloud Services usage high relative to compute. A common misconception is treating Cloud Services as always reset-included; while typically included, you should be aware of abnormal metadata activity. Key takeaway: design workloads to avoid excessive small, metadata-heavy operations and monitor Cloud Services usage if your environment shows unusually high coordination activity. Cloud Services Costs means normally included in compute, but can be billed separately for excessive metadata or control-plane activity.. In practical terms, when the cloud services layer can be charged separately. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Cost Optimization Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizing Snowflake costs combines configuration, process, and monitoring. Start by right-sizing warehouses: select the smallest warehouse that meets job SLAs rather than defaulting to larger sizes. Use AUTO_SUSPEND with a short idle timeout so warehouses stop when idle and AUTO_RESUME so they restart on demand. Use zero-copy cloning for development and testing: clones reference the same underlying storage and you only pay for changes to the clone, dramatically reducing storage duplication. Tune queries and materialize frequent patterns to reduce compute time. Monitor usage regularly in Snowsight, focusing on credit consumption per warehouse and average storage trends. A common mistake is optimizing only one dimension; for example, making queries faster by increasing warehouse size can increase compute spend if the query frequency isn't reduced. Instead, test query tuning and materialized views first, then adjust warehouse size. screens.title: Common Cost Mistakes & Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Teams commonly make a few predictable mistakes that increase Snowflake spend. First, leaving warehouses running between jobs or overnight is a top source of unnecessary compute charges; enable AUTO_SUSPEND with a short timeout to avoid this. Second, over-provisioning warehouse size to mask slow queries instead of tuning queries can multiply compute costs; measure first, then tune or right-size. Third, underestimating storage impact of Time Travel and Fail-safe leads to surprise charges; remember Fail-safe is a non-configurable seven-day retention billed as storage. Fourth, duplicating data for dev/test instead of using zero-copy cloning creates avoidable storage costs. Finally, not monitoring Cloud Services usage when you have many small metadata-heavy operations can allow an unusual billing case to go unnoticed. A simple operational guard is to add regular usage reviews in your sprint or ops cadence and create minimum configuration standards: auto-suspend enabled, maximum default warehouse size, and cloning for dev. Key takeaway: set policies and verify them with Snowsight to prevent small misconfigurations from producing large bills. Which of these mistakes is most likely in your team’s workflow? Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how Snowflake’s editions and its consumption-based pricing shape what you can do and the cost you pay. Snowflake offers distinct editions — Standard, Enterprise, Business Critical, and Virtual Private Snowflake — each providing progressively stronger features for concurrency, recovery, and compliance. Understanding those differences helps you pick the right trade-off between capability and price. Equally important is Snowflake’s billing model: storage charges for average compressed data retained, compute billed as credits while virtual warehouses run, and a Cloud Services layer that normally is included but can be charged for extreme metadata activity. Throughout this chapter you’ll see concrete examples: credit rates by warehouse size, the effect of Time Travel and Fail-safe on storage, and common mistakes that lead to unexpected bills. You’ll also learn practical controls — auto-suspend, right-sizing, and zero-copy cloning — that reduce cost without sacrificing productivity. By the end, you’ll be able to map a business requirement to an edition choice and a cost-control plan. Consider which feature matters most to your organization: concurrency, compliance, or isolation?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the appropriate Snowflake edition for a given requirement, explain how storage and compute contribute to your bill, and use practical controls to limit cost. First, you will differentiate Standard, Enterprise, Business Critical, and VPS editions by features and compliance needs. For example, you'll recognize when multi-cluster warehouses or Tri-Secret Secure are required. Second, you will identify the cost drivers: average compressed storage billed per month, compute billed as credits while warehouses run, and the Cloud Services layer that usually is included but may be charged for extreme metadata use. Third, you will explain optimization strategies such as right-sizing warehouses, enabling auto-suspend, and using zero-copy cloning to avoid duplicate storage costs. Finally, you will monitor resource usage in Snowsight and interpret credit and storage charts to make decisions. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competency by checking usage charts and applying a suspension on a test warehouse. These skills help teams avoid common billing surprises while maintaining performance and compliance.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical verification steps so you can confirm you understand costs and edition trade-offs. You will locate the Usage page in Snowsight, read the credit consumption chart and storage metrics, and identify which warehouse most contributes to credits. For compute, you will verify that AUTO underscore SUSPEND is configured and experiment by suspending a test warehouse to observe credit flow. For storage, you will inspect average compressed storage and Fail-safe usage and reason how Time Travel settings change monthly storage billing. For edition selection, you will map an example requirement—high concurrency and up to 90 days of recovery—to the Enterprise edition, and map a high-compliance government requirement to VPS. Each verification is brief: check a chart, adjust a small setting, and observe the effect. These hands-on checks turn conceptual knowledge into operational skill and help prevent the common misconception that compute and Cloud Services are always inseparable in billing.

Snowflake editions are packaged service tiers that expose different features and levels of isolation to match organizational needs. At its base, the Standard edition supplies the fully managed warehouse with separate storage and compute, secure sharing, and encryption. Enterprise adds operational capabilities such as multi-cluster warehouses to handle concurrency, longer Time Travel retention up to 90 days, and materialized views to improve query performance. Business Critical layers on compliance and advanced encryption controls like Tri-Secret Secure and database failover for disaster recovery. Virtual Private Snowflake provides a fully isolated Snowflake deployment for extreme security and regulatory requirements. A practical example: a small analytics team without strict regulatory needs commonly starts on Standard to avoid paying for advanced compliance features they won't use. A bank that needs HIPAA, PCI DSS, or FedRAMP will consider Business Critical or VPS to meet audits and control encryption keys. A common misconception is thinking edition selection only affects security; in reality it also changes operational capabilities such as concurrency, recovery time windows, and metadata isolation. Key takeaway: match edition choice to real requirements — concurrency and recovery point needs, and compliance obligations — rather than choosing the highest edition by default. Which dimension—concurrency, compliance, or full isolation—matters most for your workload?

Comparing Standard and Enterprise editions helps you decide when to upgrade as usage grows. Standard provides the managed data warehouse, encryption in transit and at rest, separate storage and compute, and secure data sharing — good for smaller teams and general analytics work. Enterprise adds features for scale and recovery: multi-cluster warehouses to handle higher concurrency without queuing, longer Time Travel retention up to 90 days for extended recovery windows, and materialized views to speed frequent queries. Consider a concrete example: if an analytics team experiences frequent query queueing during business hours, Enterprise’s multi-cluster capability can spin additional compute to serve concurrent users. A misconception is assuming Enterprise only improves performance; it also extends recovery options and supports different operational patterns like larger, more concurrent workloads. Another common pitfall is over-provisioning: upgrading before you measure concurrency or Time Travel needs can lead to unnecessary spend. Key takeaway: measure concurrency and recovery requirements first, and then apply Enterprise capabilities where real demand exists. Which workload metric will you check to justify an upgrade? Business Critical edition focuses on advanced security and compliance for regulated industries. It includes support for standards like HIPAA, PCI DSS, and FedRAMP and provides stronger controls including Tri-Secret Secure and client-side encryption options. Tri-Secret Secure gives you additional control over encryption key management so an organization can meet strict key-handling requirements. Business Critical also includes database failover and failback to improve business continuity. A concrete use case is a healthcare provider that must meet HIPAA rules and control encryption keys; Business Critical offers the features and contractual support to align operations to those obligations. Storage cost in Snowflake is based on the average amount of compressed data you store per month. That monthly average includes live table data, historical data retained for Time Travel, and data stored for Fail-safe. For example, storing 10 terabytes means you are billed for 10 TB of storage regardless of how often that data is queried.
